title: Excerpta ex Operibus Augustini
author: Eugippius
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0119.stoa003.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: I. 1. Liber ad Hieronymum presbyterum de sententia Iacobi, qua dicit: si totam quis legem seruauerit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus; cum idem dicat: in multis enim offendimus omnes. in quo libro de quattuor uirtutibus, prudentia, temperantia, fortitudine, iustitia, diligentissime disputauit.
passages.english: I. 1. A book to the priest Jerome on the saying of James in which he says: "If anyone keeps the whole law but stumbles in one [point], he has become guilty of all," although the same [James] says: "For in many things we all stumble." In this book he discussed most carefully the four virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice.

passages.original: IIII. 4. De quattuor affectionibus, quas a Cicerone perturbationes, ab aliis passiones appellatas Vergilius homini propter carnem inesse putat, cum his diabolus quoque
passages.english: IIII. 4. On the four affections, called perturbations by Cicero and passions by others, which Virgil thinks are present in man because of the flesh, [and that] the devil also [...] with these
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; "cum his diabolus quoque" is incomplete.

passages.original: CLV. 171. Quomodo Porphyrii definitio, qua beatis animis putat corpus omne fugiendum, ipsius Platonis sententia destruatur, qui dicit summum deum dis promisisse ut numquam corporibus exuerentur.
passages.english: CLV. 171. How the definition of Porphyry, by which he holds that every body is to be fled by blessed souls, is destroyed by the opinion of Plato himself, who says that the supreme god promised the gods that they would never be stripped of their bodies.

passages.original: IIII DE QVATTVOR AFFECTIONIBVS, QVAS A CICERONE PERTVR- BATIONES, AB ALIIS PASSIONES APPELLATAS VERGILIVS HOMINI PROPTER CARNEM INESSE DIXIT, IN LIBRO XIIII DE CIVITATE DEI INTER CETERA SIC EXPONIT.
passages.english: IIII. On the four affections, called perturbations by Cicero and passions by others, which Virgil said are present in man because of the flesh: in the fourteenth book of The City of God, among other things, he sets [them] out thus.

passages.original: ideo quando in forma serui ut mediator esset infra angelos esse uoluit, in forma dei supra angelos mansit: idem in inferioribus uia uitae qui in superioribus uita. non enim uerum est quod idem Platonicus ait Platonem dixisse: nullus deus miscetur homini; et hoc praecipuum eorum sublimitatis ait esse specimen quod nulla attrectatione hominum contaminantur. ergo daemones contaminari fatetur, et ideo eos a quibus contaminantur mundare non possunt omnesque immundi pariter fiunt, et daemones contrectatione hominum et homines cultu daemonum.
passages.english: Therefore, when in the form of a servant he willed to be below the angels in order to be mediator, in the form of God he remained above the angels: the same [one] is the way of life among those below who is the life among those above. For it is not true, what the same Platonist says Plato said: "No god mingles with man"; and he says that this is the chief proof of their sublimity, that they are not defiled by any contact with men. So he admits that the demons are defiled, and therefore they cannot cleanse those by whom they are defiled, and all alike become unclean, the demons by contact with men and men by the worship of demons.
passages.notes: "The same Platonist" is Apuleius (in Augustine's City of God), though not named here.

passages.original: an potius locutionis est scripturarum, ut aeternum appellent cuius rei finis non constituitur aut non ita fit, ut deinceps non sit faciendum, quantum pertinet ad curam uel potestatem facientis; sicut ait Horatius: seruiet aeternum qui paruo nesciet uti. non enim potest in aeternum seruire, cuius ipsa uita, qua seruit, aeterna esse non potest. quod testimonium non adhiberem, nisi locutionis esset; uerborum quippe illi sunt nobis auctores, non rerum uel sententiarum.
passages.english: Or is it rather an idiom of the Scriptures, that they call eternal that thing whose end is not fixed, or which is not done in such a way that it must not be done thereafter, as far as concerns the care or power of the doer; as Horace says: "He will be a slave eternally who will not know how to use little." For he cannot be a slave for eternity whose very life, in which he is a slave, cannot be eternal. I would not bring in this testimony were it not a matter of idiom; for those [authors] are our authorities for words, not for things or opinions.

passages.original: cum uero illa quae magis dolere potest non possit mori, quid momenti affert, cur illa corpora, quoniam futura sunt in doloribus, ideo etiam moritura esse credamus? dixerunt quidem Platonici ex terrenis corporibus moribundisque membris esse animae et metuere et cupere. et . dolere atque gaudere. unde Vergilius: "hinc" inquit — id est ex moribundis terreni corporis membris — "metuunt cupiuntque, dolent gaudentque." sed conuicimus eos in duodecimo huius operis libro, habere animas. secundum ipsos ab omni etiam corporis labe purgatas diram cupiditatem, qua "rursus incipiunt in corpora uelle reuerti." ubi autem potest esse cupiditas, profecto etiam dolor potest.
passages.english: But since that [soul] which is more capable of pain cannot die, what weight does it carry that we should believe those bodies, because they are going to be in pains, are therefore also going to die? The Platonists indeed said that it is from earthly bodies and dying members that the soul has both fear and desire, and pain and joy. Hence Virgil: "From this," he says — that is, from the dying members of the earthly body — "they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice." But we have refuted them in the twelfth book of this work [by showing that] souls, according to them, even when purged of every stain of the body, have a dire desire by which "they begin again to wish to return into bodies." But where there can be desire, surely there can also be pain.
passages.notes: "et . dolere": stray dot omitted. The punctuation "habere animas. secundum ipsos" seems faulty; read as one clause. The reference to the "twelfth" book may be an error (the argument is in Book 14).

passages.original: Sic autem quidam eorum, contra quos defendimus ciuitatem dei, iniustum putant, ut pro peccatis quamlibet magnis paruo scilicet tempore perpetratis, poena quisque damnetur aeterna, quasi ullius id umquam iustitia legis attendat, ut tanta mora temporis quisque puniatur, quanta mora temporis unde puniretur admisit. octo genera poenarum in Legibus scribit esse Tullius, damnum, uincla, uerbera, talionem, ignominiam, exilium, mortem, seruitutem. quid horum est quod in breue tempus pro cuiusque peccati celeritate coartetur, ut tanta uindicetur morula, quanta deprehenditur perpetratum, nisi forte talio ?
passages.english: Thus, however, some of those against whom we are defending the city of God think it unjust that anyone should be condemned to eternal punishment for sins, however great, committed of course in a short time, as if the justice of any law ever took into account that each should be punished for as long a span of time as he took to commit that for which he is punished. Tully writes in the Laws that there are eight kinds of punishment: fine, chains, beating, retaliation, disgrace, exile, death, slavery. Which of these is compressed into a short time according to the swiftness of each sin, so that it is punished for just as brief a while as it is found to have been committed in, unless perhaps retaliation?

passages.original: et alia, quae ad hoc pertinentia in libro uicesimo posui, sine quae non posui et tamen in eisdem litteris scripta sunt, uenient et haec, sicut ista uenerunt, quae increduli non putabant esse uentura. idem quippe deus utraque promisit, utraque uentura esse praedixit, quem perhorrescunt nomina paganorum etiam teste Porphyrio, nobilissimo philosopho paganorum.
passages.english: And the other things pertaining to this which I set down in the twentieth book, or which I did not set down and yet are written in the same writings, these too will come, just as those have come which unbelievers did not think would come. For the same God promised both, foretold that both would come, whom the deities of the pagans dread, as even Porphyry, the most noble philosopher of the pagans, testifies.
passages.notes: "sine" read as "siue"; "nomina" (names) is probably a misreading of "numina" (deities), translated as such.

passages.original: "magis est" inquit "in Romulo admirandum, quod ceteri, qui dei ex hominibus facti esse dicuntur, minus eruditis hominum saeculis fuerunt, ut fingendi procliuis esset ratio, cum imperiti facile ad credendum impellerentur, Romuli autem aetatem minus his sescentis annis iam inueteratis litteris atque doctrinis omnique illo antiquo ex inculta hominum uita errore sublato fuisse cernimus." et paulo post de eodem Romulo ita loquitur, quod ad hunc pertinet sensum: "ex quo intellegi potest" inquit "permultis annis ante Homerum fuisse quam Romulum, ut iam doctis hominibus ac temporibus ipsis eruditis ad fingendum uix quicquam esset loci. antiquitas enim recepit fabulas fictas etiam nonnumquam incondite; haec aetas autem iam exculta praesertim eludens omne, quod fieri non potest, respuit." unus e numero doctissimorum hominum idemque eloquentissimus omnium Marcus Tullius Cicero propterea dicit diuinitatem Romuli mirabiliter creditam, quod erudita iam tempora fuerunt, quae falsitatem non reciperent fabularum.
passages.english: "It is more to be wondered at in Romulus," he says, "that the others who are said to have become gods from men lived in less learned ages of mankind, so that there was a ready occasion for invention, since the unskilled were easily driven to believe; but we see that the age of Romulus was less than six hundred years ago, when letters and learning had already grown old and all that ancient error arising from the uncultivated life of men had been removed." And a little later he speaks thus about the same Romulus, to this effect: "From this it can be understood," he says, "that Homer lived very many years before Romulus, so that, men now being learned and the times themselves educated, there was scarcely any room for invention. For antiquity accepted invented fables, sometimes even crude ones; but this age, already refined, especially mocking everything that cannot happen, rejected [them]." One of the number of the most learned men, and likewise the most eloquent of all, Marcus Tullius Cicero, says that the divinity of Romulus was wonderfully believed for this reason, that the times were already learned, which would not accept the falsehood of fables.

passages.original: Sed Porphyrius ait, inquiunt, ut beata sit anima, corpus esse omne fugiendum. nihil ergo prodest, quia incorruptibile diximus futurum corpus, si anima beata non erit, nisi omne corpus effugerit. sed iam et hinc in libro memorato quantum oportuit disputaui.
passages.english: But Porphyry says, they claim, that for the soul to be happy, every body must be fled. It is therefore of no use that we have said the future body will be incorruptible, if the soul will not be happy unless it has escaped every body. But I have already discussed this too, as much as was needed, in the book mentioned.
passages.notes: The 'book mentioned' presumably refers to an earlier book of the City of God (Book 13); the reference is not given in the excerpt.

passages.original: ubi etiam illud euertit quod dicunt, quoniam est impossibilis, ideo resurrectionem carnis non esse credendam. apertissime quippe iuxta eundem philosophum, ubi dis a se factis promisit deus non factus immortalitatem, quod impossibile est se dixit esse facturum. sic enim eum locuturum narrat Plato: "quoniam estis orti" inquit "immortales esse et indissolubiles non potestis; non tamen dissoluemini neque uos ulla mortis fata periment nec erunt ualentiora quam consilium meum, quod maius est uinculum ad perpetuitatem uestram quam illa quibus estis colligati." si non solum absurdi, sed surdi non sunt qui haec audiunt, non utique dubitant dis factis ab illo deo, qui eos fecit, secundum Platonem quod est impossibile fuisse promissum.
passages.english: There he also overturns what they say, that the resurrection of the flesh should not be believed because it is impossible. For quite plainly, according to that same philosopher, where the uncreated God promised immortality to the gods made by him, he said that he would do what is impossible. For Plato relates that he spoke thus: "Since you have come into being," he says, "you cannot be immortal and indissoluble; yet you will not be dissolved, nor will any fates of death destroy you, nor will they be stronger than my purpose, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those by which you are bound together." If those who hear this are not only not absurd but not deaf, they surely do not doubt that, according to Plato, what is impossible was promised to the gods made by that God who made them.
passages.notes: Wordplay absurdi/surdi ('absurd'/'deaf') is lost in English. The subject of 'he overturns' is unclear in the excerpt; it may be Plato, or the argument itself.

passages.original: quid adhuc quod promisit deus, quod deo promittenti credidit mundus, qui etiam ipse promissus est crediturus, esse impossibile clamant, quando quidem nos deum, qui etiam secundum Platonem facit impossibilia, id facturum esse clamamus P non ergo, ut beatae sint animae, corpus est omne fugiendum, sed corpus incorruptibile recipiendum. et in quo conuenientius incorruptibili corpore laetabuntur, quam in quo corruptibili gemuerunt? sic enim non in eis erit illa dira cupiditas, quam posuit ex Platone Vergilius, ubi ait: rursus et incipiant in corpora uelle reuerti; sic, inquam, cupiditatem reuertendi ad corpora non habebunt, cum corpora, in quae reuerti cupiunt, secum habebunt et sic habebunt, ut numquam non habeant, numquam ea prorsus uel exiguum quodlibet tempus ulla morte deponant.
passages.english: Why do they still cry out that what God has promised is impossible, what the world believed when God promised it, the world that was itself also promised as going to believe, since we cry out that God, who even according to Plato does impossible things, will do it? So it is not that every body must be fled for souls to be happy, but that an incorruptible body must be received. And in what incorruptible body will they rejoice more fittingly than in the one in which, when it was corruptible, they groaned? For thus there will not be in them that dreadful desire which Virgil took from Plato, where he says: "and they may begin to wish to return again into bodies." Thus, I say, they will have no desire to return to bodies, since they will have with them the bodies to which they desire to return, and will have them in such a way that they never lack them, and never lay them down at all through any death, even for the briefest time.
passages.notes: A stray 'P' after 'clamamus' appears to be a scanning or marginal mark and is omitted; the first sentence is read as a question.

passages.original: rursus quod uerum uidit Porphyrius dedisset Platoni, numquam redituras ad miserias corruptibilis corporis animas sanctas, ut non singuli haec singula, sed ambo et singuli utrumque dicerent: puto quod uiderent esse iam consequens, ut redirent animae ad corpora et talia reciperent corpora, in quibus beate atque immortaliter uiuerent. quoniam secundum Platonem etiam sanctae animae ad humana corpora redibunt, secundum Porphyrium ad mala huius mundi sanctae animae non redibunt. dicat itaque cum Platone Porphyrius: "redibunt ad corpora;" dicat Plato cum Porphyrio: "non redibunt ad mala": et ad ea corpora redire consentient, in quibus nulla patiantur mala. haec itaque non erunt nisi illa quae promittit deus, beatas animas in aeternum cum sua aeterna carne iacturas.
passages.english: Again, if Porphyry had granted Plato what he saw to be true, that holy souls will never return to the miseries of a corruptible body, so that they did not each say each of these things separately, but both together and each of them said both, I think they would see that it now follows that souls return to bodies and receive such bodies as those in which they might live happily and immortally. For according to Plato even holy souls will return to human bodies; according to Porphyry holy souls will not return to the evils of this world. So let Porphyry say with Plato, "They will return to bodies"; let Plato say with Porphyry, "They will not return to evils"; and they will agree that they return to those bodies in which they suffer no evils. These, then, will be none other than those which God promises, [saying] that happy souls will live for ever with their own eternal flesh.
passages.notes: 'iacturas' is evidently corrupt; read as 'acturas' (will live/spend [life]), as the sense requires.

passages.original: Nonnulli nostri propter quoddam praeclarissimum loquendi genus et propter nonnulla, quae ueraciter sensit, amantes Platonem dicunt eum aliquid simile nobis etiam de mortuorum resurrectione sensisse. quod quidem sic tangit in libris de re publica Tullius, ut eum lusisse potius quam quod id uerum esse affirmet dicere uoluisse.
passages.english: Some of our people, loving Plato for a certain most distinguished manner of speaking and for some things that he truly perceived, say that he also held something similar to us concerning the resurrection of the dead. Tullius touches on this in his books On the Republic in such a way that he seems to have meant that Plato was playing rather than meaning to say that he affirmed it to be true.
passages.notes: Tullius = Cicero. The second sentence is awkward in the Latin; rendered by its evident sense.

passages.original: sed isti auctores talem resurrectionem corporis factam fuisse narrarunt, quales fuerunt eorum, quos resurrexisse nouimus et huic quidem redditos uitae, sed non eo modo, at non morerentur ulterius. mirabilius autem quidam Marcus Varro ponit in libris, quos conscripsit de gente populi Romani, cuius putaui uerba ipsa ponenda. "genethliaci quidam scripserunt" inquit "esse in renascendis hominibus quam appellant παλγγενεσίαν Graeci;
passages.english: But these authors related that a resurrection of the body took place of such a kind as was that of those whom we know to have risen again and to have been restored indeed to this life, but not in such a way that they would not die any more. But a certain Marcus Varro sets down something more wonderful in the books which he wrote on the race of the Roman people, whose very words I thought should be quoted. "Certain genethliaci [casters of nativities]," he says, "have written that there is in the rebirth of men what the Greeks call *palingenesia* [rebirth];
passages.notes: "at non" read as "ut non"; "παλγγενεσίαν" is a scanning error for παλιγγενεσίαν.

passages.original: quapropter Plato et Porphyrius uel potius quicumque illos diligunt et adhuc uiuunt, si nobis consentiunt etiam sanctas animas ad corpora redituras, sicut ait Plato, nec tamen ad mala ulla redituras, sicut ait Porphyrius, ut ex his fiat consequens, quod fides praedicat christiana, talia corpora recepturas, in quibus sine ullo modo in aeternum feliciter uiuant, assumant etiam hoc de Varrone, ut ad eadem corpora redeant, in quibus antea fuerunt, et apud eos tota quaestio de carnis in aeternum resurrectione soluetur.
passages.english: Therefore Plato and Porphyry, or rather any who love them and are still alive, if they agree with us that even holy souls will return to bodies, as Plato says, and yet will not return to any evils, as Porphyry says, so that from these it follows, as the Christian faith proclaims, that they will receive such bodies in which they may live happily for ever without any [evil], let them also take this from Varro, that they return to the same bodies in which they were before, and among them the whole question of the resurrection of the flesh for ever will be solved.
passages.notes: 'sine ullo modo' seems corrupt; probably 'sine ullo malo' ('without any evil'), which is translated.

passages.original: nam secundum interpretes septuaginta ista sunt ad Giezi uerba prophetae: nonne cor meum iuit tecum, quando conuersus est uir de curru in obuiam tibi et accepisti pecuniam? et cetera; sicut autem ex hebraeo interpretatus est presbyter Hieronymus: nonne cor meum, inquit, in praesentia erat, quando reuersus est homo de curru suo in occursum tibi? corde suo ergo se dixit hoc uidisse propheta, adiuto quidem mirabiliter nullo dubitante diuinitus.
passages.english: For according to the Seventy translators, these are the prophet's words to Gehazi: "Did not my heart go with you, when the man turned from the chariot to meet you, and you took the money?" and so on; but as the presbyter Jerome translated from the Hebrew: "Was not my heart present," he says, "when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you?" So the prophet said he saw this with his heart, which was, no one doubts, wonderfully aided by God.

passages.original: in quo genere fingendi humana etiam dicta uel facta inrationabilibus animantibus et rebus sensu carentibus homines addiderunt, ut eius modi fictis narrationibus, sed ueracibus significationibus quod uellent commendatius intimarent. nec aput auctores tantum saecularium litterarum, ut apud Horatium, mus loquitur muri et mustela uulpiculae, ut per narrationem fictam ad id quod agitur uerax significatio referatur; unde et Aesopi tales fabulas ad eum finem relatas nullus tam ineruditus fuit, qui putaret appellanda mendacia.
passages.english: In this kind of fiction people have attributed human words or deeds even to irrational animals and to things lacking sense, so that by fictitious narratives of this sort, but with truthful meanings, they might convey what they wished more persuasively. And not only among the authors of secular literature, as in Horace, where a mouse speaks to a mouse and a weasel to a little fox, so that through a fictitious narrative a truthful meaning is referred to the matter at hand; hence no one has been so uneducated as to think that such fables of Aesop, directed to that end, should be called lies.

passages.original: aut quomodo salui fiunt per aquam qui sancto baptismate male utentes, cum uideantur esse intus, usque in finem uitae in flagitiosis et perditis moribus perseuerant? aut quomodo non sunt per aquam saluati quos in praeteritum cum eo baptismate, quod in haeresi acceperant, in ecclesiam simpliciter admissos Cyprianus ipse commemorat ? eadem quippe arcae unitas eos saluos fecit, in qua nemo nisi per aquam saluatus est. ipse enim dicit: potens est dominus misericordia sua indulgentiam dare et eos qui ad ecclesiam simpliciter admissi in ecclesia dormierunt ab ecclesiae suae muneribus non separare. si non per aquam, quomodo in arca? si non in arca, quomodo in ecclesia? si autem in ecclesia, utique in arca;
passages.english: Or how are those saved through water who, misusing holy baptism, though they seem to be inside, persist until the end of life in shameful and depraved ways? Or how were those not saved through water whom Cyprian himself mentions as having in the past been simply admitted into the church with the baptism they had received in heresy? For the same unity of the ark saved them, in which no one was saved except through water. For he himself says: "The Lord is able by his mercy to grant pardon, and not to separate from the gifts of his church those who, simply admitted to the church, have fallen asleep in the church." If not through water, how in the ark? If not in the ark, how in the church? But if in the church, then certainly in the ark;

passages.original: sed quodlibet horum esset, etiam in hoc libro apparuit trinitatis aequalitas et non deus triplex, sed trinitas, nec quasi aliquid duplum esse patrem et filium ad simplum spiritum sanctum, ubi nec tria plus aliquid sunt quam unum horum. disputatum est etiam, quomodo possit intellegi quod ait Hilarius episcopus: aeternitas in patre, species in imagine, usus in munere. in septimo quaestio, quae dilata fuerat, explicatur, ita ut deus, qui genuit filium, non solum sit pater uirtutis et sapientiae suae, sed etiam ipse uirtus atque sapientia, sic et spiritus sanctus, nec tamen simul tres sint uirtutes aut tres sapientiae, sed una uirtus et una sapientia, sicut unus deus et una essentia.
passages.english: But whichever of these it were, in this book too the equality of the Trinity has been shown, and that God is not threefold but a Trinity, and that the Father and Son are not something double as against the Holy Spirit as single, since three are not anything more than one of them. It was also discussed how one may understand what Bishop Hilary says: "Eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift." In the seventh, the question that had been deferred is explained, so that God who begot the Son is not only the Father of his power and wisdom, but is himself also power and wisdom, and so too the Holy Spirit; and yet they are not together three powers or three wisdoms, but one power and one wisdom, as one God and one essence.

passages.original: dicit enim ciuitatem nescio quam — non enim nomen recolo — locasse apud tres artifices terna simulacra Musarum, quod in templo Apollinis donum poneret, ut quisquis artificum pulchriora formasset, ab illo potissimum electa emerent. ita contigisse, ut opera sua quoque illa artifices aeque pulchra explicarent, et placuisse ciuitati omnes nouem atque omnes esse emtas, ut in Apollinis templo dedicarentur. quibus postea dicit Hesiodum poetam imposuisse uocabula. non ergo Iuppiter nouem Musas genuit, sed tres fabri ternas creauerunt. tres autem non propterea illa ciuitas locauerat, quia in somnis eas uiderat aut tot se cuiusquam illorum oculis demonstrauerant, sed quia facile erat animaduertere omnem sonum, quae materies cantilenarum est, triformem esse natura.
passages.english: For he says that some city or other (for I do not recall the name) contracted with three artisans for three statues each of the Muses, to place as a gift in the temple of Apollo, so that whichever of the artisans had fashioned the more beautiful ones, from him above all they would buy those chosen. It so happened that the artisans each turned out those works of theirs equally beautiful, and that all nine pleased the city and all were bought, to be dedicated in the temple of Apollo. To these, he says, the poet Hesiod afterwards gave names. So Jupiter did not beget nine Muses; rather, three craftsmen created three each. And that city had contracted for three not because it had seen them in dreams, or because that many had shown themselves to the eyes of any of those [citizens], but because it was easy to notice that all sound, which is the material of songs, is by nature threefold.
passages.notes: "quod ... poneret": the relative refers loosely to the commission/gift; rendered by sense. "quae materies": the feminine relative agrees with materies rather than sonum.

passages.original: Sed siue ita se habeat quod Varro rettulit, siue non ita, nos tamen non propter superstitionem profanorum debemus musicam fugere, si quid inde utile ad intellegendas sanctas scripturas rapere potuerimus, nec ad illorum theatricas nugas conuerti, si aliquid de citharis et de organis, quod ad spiritalia capienda ualeat, disputemus.
passages.english: But whether what Varro reported is so or not so, we nevertheless ought not to flee from music on account of the superstition of the profane, if we can seize from it anything useful for understanding the holy scriptures; nor are we turning to their theatrical trifles if we discuss something about lyres and organs that may help toward grasping spiritual things.

passages.original: uelut cum intuentes tabulam aut parietem dicimus: "ille Cicero est, ille Sallustius; ille Achilles, ille Hector; hoc flumen Simois, illa Roma", cum aliud nihil sint quam picturae, imagines. unde cherubin cum sint caelestes potestates, fictae tamen ex metallo, quod imperauit deus, super arcam testamenti magnae rei significandae gratia non aliud quam cherubin illa quoque figmenta uocitantur. item quisquis uidet somnium, non dicit: „uidi imaginem Augustini aut Simpliciani," sed: "uidi Augustinum et Simplicianum", cum eo tempore, quo tale aliquid uidit, nos ignoraremus. usque adeo manifestum est non ipsos homines, sed imagines eorum uideri. et Pharao spicas se dixit uidisse in somnis et boues, non spicarum aut boum imagines. si igitur liquido constat nominibus earum rerum, quarum imagines sunt, easdem imagines appellari, non mirum est, quod scriptura dicit Samuhelem uisum, etiam si forte imago Samuhelis apparuit machinamento eius qui transfigurat se uelut in angelum lucis et ministros suos uelut ministros iustitiae.
passages.english: as when, looking at a panel or a wall, we say: "That is Cicero, that is Sallust; that is Achilles, that is Hector; this river is the Simois, that is Rome," although they are nothing other than paintings, images. Hence, although the cherubim are heavenly powers, yet those figures too which were fashioned from metal, as God commanded, over the ark of the covenant for the sake of signifying a great matter, are called nothing other than cherubim. Likewise, whoever sees a dream does not say, "I saw an image of Augustine or of Simplician," but, "I saw Augustine and Simplician," although at the time when he saw some such thing we were unaware of it. So evident is it that it is not the men themselves but their images that are seen. And Pharaoh said that he had seen ears of grain and cows in his dreams, not images of ears of grain or of cows. If, then, it is plainly established that images are called by the names of the things of which they are images, it is no wonder that Scripture says Samuel was seen, even if perhaps an image of Samuel appeared through the contrivance of him who transforms himself as if into an angel of light, and his ministers as if into ministers of righteousness.

passages.original: sed eodem ipso ferme tempore, quo id audiuimus, id est nobis apud Mediolanium constitutis, Carthaginis rhetor Eulogius, qui meus in eadem arte discipulus fuit, sicut ipse mihi, posteaquam in Africam remeauimus, rettulit, cum rhetoricos Ciceronis libros discipulis suis traderet, recensens lectionem, quam post diem fuerat traditurus, quendam locum offendit obscurum, quo non intellecto uix potuit dormire sollicitus. qua nocte somnianti ego illi quod non intellegebat exposui, immo non ego, sed imago mea nesciente me et tam longe trans mare aliquid aliud siue agente siue somniante et nihil de illius omnino curante.
passages.english: But at almost the very same time that we heard this, that is, while we were staying at Milan, Eulogius, a rhetorician of Carthage, who had been my pupil in that same art, as he himself told me after we returned to Africa, while he was teaching Cicero's books on rhetoric to his pupils, in going over the reading which he was to teach the next day, came upon a certain obscure passage; and not understanding it, he could hardly sleep for worry. That night, as he dreamed, I explained to him what he did not understand; or rather not I, but my image, without my knowing it, while I, so far away across the sea, was either doing or dreaming something else and not concerned with his affairs at all.
